# SIXTOM — full content

> you told them to use AI. nothing changed. the enablement engagement: two weeks, one team. by day 10 a named person on your team ships a real internal system, or the rest is free. $15,000 fixed. 1 team a month.

## thesis

setup was easy. what comes after isn't.

the memo went out. a few people tried it. a few more pretended to. the work looks the same. this year i've been turning ops, finance and marketing people into people who ship real systems. that's what i do for your team.

the tools got installed. the licenses got paid for. then half of marketing's week went to arguing which of three numbers is right. the glue between your apps broke and nobody noticed for a month. the one person who got good opened a 45,000-line pull request and nobody knew how to review it. the dashboard says live. nobody believes it. and it starts at the top. if leadership won't use it, the team won't either. every month it stays that way has a price: the licenses, paid for every month and opened twice. the glue, failing quietly until a customer finds out. the one who got good, shipping fast with no guardrails until prod breaks. that part is fixable in two weeks.

## the offer — one engagement, everything in it

i sit with your team for two weeks and we build something real, on your data, in your repo. everything in the engagement, and what it'd cost you piecemeal:

### the diagnosis

- adoption teardown — who's using it, where it's stuck, what's quietly broken — $1,500
- one metric, one definition — the number everyone argues about gets a single source of truth — $3,000

### the build

- the system — a named person on your team ships a real internal tool, on your data — core
- glue → code — one fragile automation chain rebuilt as code you can read, with alerts and a last-run time — $4,000
- honest status — every "live" badge shows when it last synced — $1,000

### the guardrails

- permissions + review gate — nothing reaches production without passing review — $3,000
- repo rules — one branch per tool, hooks, shared instructions. a 45,000-line PR can't happen — $2,500
- customer data off desktops — it lives somewhere with access control, not on a laptop — $2,000

### the people

- hands-on onboarding — everyone on the team set up and shipping. by the tenth person it takes one sitting — $4,000
- the tracing-paper session — git and review, explained so it sticks for people who never wanted to learn git — $1,500
- the leadership session — the people at the top use it first, so the team follows — $2,000

### the close (bonuses land by day 30)

- shipped by day 10 — you own 100% of it — included
- day-30 check-in — what stuck, what didn't — $500
- the runbook + Loom library — so the next hire onboards without me — $1,500
- the 90-day map — the next three systems worth building, in order — $1,500

**total value: $28,000+. you pay: $15,000 fixed. half up front, half on day 10.**

a consultancy quotes six figures and delivers a deck. a workshop is half a day and a recording nobody watches. this is two weeks, and something running when i leave.

## the guarantee

your person ships by day 10, or the rest is free.

and there's a floor under it: day 5, we both look at it. if we can both see it won't ship in scope, we stop there. you keep everything we built and pay only for the time used. the risk is mine to carry, not yours.

## the teardown

$1,500, credited in full against the engagement if you book one within 30 days. i look at how your team works today: the tools, the automations, the numbers people argue about. you get a 10-minute Loom and a written list of what's stuck and what i'd fix first. you keep it whether or not we work together, and i'll tell you if you don't need me.

## proof — inside a consumer brand

since july i've run 22 onboarding sessions across ops, finance, marketing, wholesale and creative. into a shared repo, behind a review gate. none of them were hired to write code. by the tenth session, setup took one sitting. three glue chains are code now. one finance analyst shipped dashboards fast enough that their lead asked them to slow down. git got explained with tracing paper, and it stuck.

before this, the craft: a solo therapy practice rebuilt in 4h43m. mobile load 8.3s → 2.9s. pageviews up 185%. same hands.

## who it's for

this is for you if: you sent the memo. nothing changed · you have a team, and they aren't engineers · someone on it is curious, or already shipping without guardrails · you'd rather your people own it than rent a consultancy.

not yet if: it's just you. no team yet · you want a workshop and a recording · you want it done for you, with nobody on your side learning.

## how the two weeks go

- wk 1 · day 0: a 30-minute call. we pick the person and the system.
- days 1–7: we build it together, in your repo, on your data. a daily Loom so leadership watches it happen.
- day 5 · scope check: if it can't ship in scope, we stop here. you keep what we built.
- week 2: the guardrails go in. the rest of the team gets set up. one session with leadership.
- day 10: shipped. your person owns it. (or the rest is free.)
- day 30: check-in. what stuck, what didn't.

## FAQ

**what does sixtom do?**

you told your team to use AI and nothing changed. in two weeks, one named person on your team ships a real internal system, the fragile glue between your tools becomes code you can watch, and the guardrails hold once they get good. you own all of it.

**how much does it cost?**

$15,000 fixed. half up front, half on day 10. that buys the whole ledger on the home page, over $28,000 of itemized work. the price is the same for everyone.

**what's the guarantee?**

your person ships the system by day 10, or the remaining payment is free. there's a floor under it too: at the day-5 scope check, if we can both see it won't ship in scope, we stop. you keep everything built and pay only for the time used.

**what's the teardown?**

$1,500, credited in full against the engagement if you book one within 30 days. i look at how your team works today: the tools, the automations, the numbers people argue about. you get a 10-minute Loom and a written list of what's stuck and what i'd fix first. you keep it whether or not we work together, and i'll tell you if you don't need me.

**how long does it take?**

two weeks. shipped by day 10. one team a month, by appointment.

**does my team need to be technical?**

no. the people i onboard work in ops, finance, marketing and wholesale. none of them were hired to write code. they need a setup that works, a review gate, and someone to explain git with tracing paper.

**how many clients do you take?**

one team a month, by appointment. that's the whole model. you get my full attention, not a queue. when the seat's taken, the waitlist is open.

**what happens after the two weeks?**

you own everything: the system, the repo, the runbook. there's a day-30 check-in to see what stuck. if you want me back for the next system, we talk then.

**who's behind sixtom?**

Salvatore (Sam) D'Angelo, lead engineer at Made In Cookware (multi-million visitors a month), formerly at Rhone. sixtom is the solo practice.

**is it remote?**

yes. working sessions over video, a daily Loom, and everything lands in your repo. no standups.

## case study — garden party

a 1:1 port of threesam.com from Next.js to SvelteKit. five hours of build time. bundle size dropped 40%. every Lighthouse score went up. full writeup at https://sixtom.com/log/garden-party.

the premise: take a 30-route personal site (canvas sketches, video heroes, real-time data feeds, the works) and port it to SvelteKit — the framework i prefer and ship freelance, just never at the day job. same routes, same sketches, same aesthetic — different runtime. two questions answered honestly: is a 1:1 port across frameworks possible, and is it worth it?
